segments.text: [style: brisk, clear, architectural voice; steady studio cadence] Book Two, Proposition Four. If a segment be cut at random, the square on the whole is equal to the squares on the segments and twice the rectangle contained by the segments. Let the segment A B be cut at random at C.

segments.text: [style: luminous, deductive geometric clarity] Because C F is parallel to A D, the exterior angle C G B equals the interior angle A D B by One Twenty-Nine. And since A B equals A D, angle A D B equals angle A B D by One Five. Therefore angle C G B equals angle G B C, so side B C equals C G by One Six, and by One Thirty-Four all four sides of C G K B are equal. Moreover, since C G is parallel to B K and angle K B C is right, all four angles of C G K B are right angles. Thus C G K B is the square on B C, and for the same reason H F is the square on H G, which equals A C. Now the complements A G and G E are equal, and since C G equals B C, each is the rectangle contained by A C and B C, so together they equal twice that rectangle. Adding the two squares H F and C K, the four areas compose the whole square A D E B. Therefore, the square on A B equals the squares on A C and B C plus twice the rectangle contained by A C and B C. Which was to be proved.

segments.text: [style: reflective, scholarly, architectural synthesis] Proposition Two Four is the geometric archetype of the binomial square: the square of a plus b equals a squared plus b squared plus two a b. Rather than multiplying symbols, Euclid dissects the square along its diagonal into two squares about the diameter and two equal rectangular complements. In the GEOMETOR G-Index, node G eighty-five unites eleven prerequisites across forty-eight ancestor nodes—combining isosceles triangle symmetry, parallel transversals, and parallelogram complements into a cornerstone of Book Ten's theory of irrationals.
